name: i3
summary: A reparenting X11 tiling window manager that models managed windows as a hierarchical container tree, routes X events and keyboard bindings into commands, and maintains explicit workspace, layout, and rendering state.

features.name: X11 reparenting window-manager boundary
features.description: i3 owns the X11 window-management policy boundary, receives X events and requests, reparents managed client windows into frame and container structures, and controls mapped visibility and focus.
benefits: Makes window management policy explicit above the X server
Can manage existing X11 clients without requiring client-side tiling support
costs: The manager is coupled to X11 event and reparenting semantics
A window-manager failure removes policy and session control even though the X server may remain alive

features.name: Container-tree layout model
features.description: i3 represents outputs, workspaces, containers, and windows as a tree; split, tabbed, stacked, and floating layouts derive geometry and focus from tree structure and commands.
benefits: Supports predictable nested tiling and explicit focus traversal
Makes layout and workspace changes serializable through commands and IPC
costs: Tree mutations must preserve parent, focus, and geometry invariants
Complex nesting can make user intent and recovery from invalid layouts harder to diagnose

features.name: Keyboard binding and X-event routing
features.description: i3 grabs configured key combinations, processes keyboard and pointer-related X events, and translates them into commands that act on focused containers, workspaces, and windows.
benefits: Provides deterministic keyboard-driven control over the tree
Allows input actions to share the same command semantics as IPC clients
costs: Key grabs and modifier state depend on X server and client interactions
Input configuration errors can prevent commands without invalidating the layout tree

features.name: Workspace, output, and X-resource model
features.description: i3 tracks workspaces and output assignments alongside X windows, frame windows, pixmaps, borders, and geometry; mapping and rendering decisions are derived from this managed-resource state.
benefits: Separates logical workspace membership from physical X window resources
Supports multi-output placement, workspace visibility, and configurable borders
costs: X resource lifetime and output changes require careful cleanup and remapping
Server resource exhaustion or stale client state can distort the logical tree

features.name: IPC command/event and lifecycle boundary
features.description: i3 exposes commands, subscriptions, and tree/event replies over IPC while processing X client lifecycle events; a managed window can disappear or reject a request without necessarily invalidating unrelated workspace state, whereas X or manager failures have broader scope.
benefits: Makes automation and state observation available without scraping presentation
Separates per-window lifecycle failures from many logical workspace transitions
costs: IPC consumers must interpret event ordering and command failures
X server and window-manager failures can invalidate broad portions of resource state

mathematical_views.question: How do X clients, frame windows, containers, workspaces, outputs, and server resources connect under reparenting management?
assumptions: X resources and i3 containers are typed nodes
Events and commands are directed transitions
The model abstracts X protocol wire details

mathematical_views.question: Which tiling, tabbed, stacked, floating, focus, and workspace states are reachable under i3 commands and client events?
assumptions: Containers form a rooted tree beneath outputs and workspaces
Geometry is derived from layout and available output rectangles
Rendering is abstracted from tree transitions

mathematical_views.question: What logical state survives a client destroy, X resource failure, IPC error, output change, or manager restart?
assumptions: Client lifecycle and manager lifecycle are distinct
Resource cleanup can remove a window while retaining workspace state
This is a candidate state model rather than a recovery guarantee

benefits: Centralized policy can manage unmodified X11 clients
costs: Behavior depends on X11 reparenting and event semantics

benefits: Nested layouts and focus are explicit and scriptable
costs: Tree invariants increase mutation and debugging complexity

benefits: Keyboard commands provide direct deterministic tree control
costs: X grabs and modifier state can conflict with clients and configuration

benefits: Logical workspaces can be assigned independently of physical windows
costs: X resource cleanup and server limits add failure modes

benefits: External tools can inspect and manipulate the tree through IPC
costs: Event ordering and broad X failure scope complicate clients
